    <item>
      <title>LGBTQ+ people go into hiding in Senegal as hundreds are arrested</title>
      <link>https://www.theguardian.com/global-development/2026/oct/15/senegal-homosexuality-criminalised-anti-lgbtq-arrests-hiv-testing-human-rights-watch</link>
      <description><p>At least 320 people detained for ‘acts against nature’ after law criminalising homosexuality toughened, HRW reports</p><p>Mass arrests, forced HIV testing and barriers to legal representation are part of an escalating crackdown against LGBTQ+ people in Senegal, according to a <a href="https://www.hrw.org/news/2026/10/12/senegal-brutal-crackdown-violates-lgbt-peoples-rights">new report</a>.</p><p>More than 320 individuals have been arrested and detained on allegations of “acts against nature” since February, <a href="https://www.hivjustice.net/cases/senegal-crackdown-on-lgbtq-people-intensifies-with-multiple-arrests/">according to HIV Justice Network</a>, an organisation quoted in the Human Rights Watch (HRW) report. Among these, at least 84 were charged with “voluntary HIV transmission”, solely on the basis of their HIV status.</p> <a href="https://www.theguardian.com/global-development/2026/oct/15/senegal-homosexuality-criminalised-anti-lgbtq-arrests-hiv-testing-human-rights-watch">Continue reading...</a></description>
      <category domain="https://www.theguardian.com/global-development/global-development">Global development</category>
      <category domain="https://www.theguardian.com/world/senegal">Senegal</category>
      <category domain="https://www.theguardian.com/world/lgbt-rights">LGBTQ+ rights</category>
      <category domain="https://www.theguardian.com/global-development/human-rights">Human rights</category>
      <category domain="https://www.theguardian.com/law/human-rights">Human rights</category>
      <category domain="https://www.theguardian.com/world/anti-rights-movement">Anti-rights movement</category>
      <category domain="https://www.theguardian.com/world/africa">Africa</category>
      <category domain="https://www.theguardian.com/world/world">World news</category>
      <category domain="https://www.theguardian.com/law/law">Law</category>
      <category domain="https://www.theguardian.com/society/aids-and-hiv">Aids and HIV</category>
      <pubDate>Thu, 15 Oct 2026 08:00:25 GMT</pubDate>
      <guid>https://www.theguardian.com/global-development/2026/oct/15/senegal-homosexuality-criminalised-anti-lgbtq-arrests-hiv-testing-human-rights-watch</guid>
      <media:content width="140" url="https://i.guim.co.uk/img/media/5d08247e565b832f183d37b676fe7def25b19c25/213_0_2500_2000/master/2500.jpg?width=140&quality=85&auto=format&fit=max&s=123bd8ecc615f6c5a01371cef3492c23">
        <media:credit scheme="urn:ebu">Photograph: Jane Hahn/AP</media:credit>
      </media:content>
      <media:content width="460" url="https://i.guim.co.uk/img/media/5d08247e565b832f183d37b676fe7def25b19c25/213_0_2500_2000/master/2500.jpg?width=460&quality=85&auto=format&fit=max&s=add472ae1a295f31eda15f295087bdb3">
        <media:credit scheme="urn:ebu">Photograph: Jane Hahn/AP</media:credit>
      </media:content>
      <media:content width="700" url="https://i.guim.co.uk/img/media/5d08247e565b832f183d37b676fe7def25b19c25/213_0_2500_2000/master/2500.jpg?width=700&quality=85&auto=format&fit=max&s=80b82662e7e790a0db106b737b3aa2cb">

      <title>Guinea-Bissau denies it has approved controversial vaccine trial in newborns</title>
      <link>https://www.theguardian.com/world/2026/oct/14/guinea-bissau-vaccine-hepatitis-b-trial-denial</link>
      <description><p>Health minister says government ‘did not authorize’ Danish-led hepatitis B trial in babies backed by RFK Jr</p><p><a href="https://www.theguardian.com/world/guinea-bissau">Guinea-Bissau</a> has not approved the controversial <a href="https://www.theguardian.com/society/hepatitis-b">hepatitis B</a> study in newborns that would be funded by the US government and private partners, the African country’s minister of health said on Tuesday.</p><p>The study, which would not investigate the safety or effectiveness of vaccines but would instead track “nonspecific” health outcomes like overall mortality or neurodevelopmental conditions, has been championed by Robert F Kennedy Jr, secretary of the US Department of Health and Human Services (HHS) and a longtime anti-vaccine activist.</p> <a href="https://www.theguardian.com/world/2026/oct/14/guinea-bissau-vaccine-hepatitis-b-trial-denial">Continue reading...</a></description>

      <title>ICJ judge Navi Pillay wins Nobel peace prize for promoting international law</title>
      <link>https://www.theguardian.com/world/2026/oct/09/navanethem-navi-pillay-wins-nobel-peace-prize</link>
      <description><p>Committee recognises work of South African who chaired UN commission that concluded Israel was guilty of genocide in Gaza</p><p></p><p>The Nobel peace prize has been awarded to Navi Pillay, the South African former UN human rights chief who chaired the UN commission <a href="https://www.theguardian.com/world/2025/sep/16/israel-committed-genocide-in-gaza-says-un-inquiry">that concluded Israel was guilty of genocide in Gaza</a>.</p><p>The Norwegian Nobel committee said Pillay, who is serving as a judge at the international court of justice (ICJ), has “shown that legal measures can help prevent acts of war and violence”.</p> <a href="https://www.theguardian.com/world/2026/oct/09/navanethem-navi-pillay-wins-nobel-peace-prize">Continue reading...</a></description>

News from the US, Europe, Asia Pacific, Africa, Middle East, America</description><link>https://www.france24.com/en/</link><lastBuildDate>Sat, 17 Oct 2026 08:12:11 GMT</lastBuildDate><atom:link href="https://www.france24.com/en/rss" rel="self" type="application/rss+xml"/><item><category>Middle East</category><title>Yemen's Houthis claim responsibility for fresh missile strike on Aden airport</title><link>https://www.france24.com/en/middle-east/20261017-yemen-s-houthis-claim-responsibility-for-fresh-missile-strike-on-aden-airport</link><description>
Yemen's Iran-aligned Houthi group claimed responsibility after two missiles struck Aden International Airport on Friday, saying they had targeted a weapons depot as well as a military command headquarters. The Aden Security Department said a Yemenia Airways flight bound for Cairo had been preparing for takeoff when the attack took place.
</description><media:thumbnail url="https://s.france24.com/media/display/8be454f8-c9ee-11f1-a86a-2d1c143cdef3/w:1024/p:16x9/AP26286485676861.jpg"/><enclosure url="https://s.france24.com/media/display/8be454f8-c9ee-11f1-a86a-2d1c143cdef3/w:1024/p:16x9/AP26286485676861.jpg" type="image/jpeg" length="0"/><guid isPermaLink="false">51d31896-c9ec-11f1-a58e-a9bb97da8e14</guid><pubDate>Sat, 17 Oct 2026 06:00:32 GMT</pubDate><source url="https://s.france24.com/media/display/8be454f8-c9ee-11f1-a86a-2d1c143cdef3/w:1024/p:16x9/AP26286485676861.jpg">© Abdulnasser Alseddik, AP</source><dc:creator>FRANCE 24</dc:creator></item><item><category>France</category><title>Live: France's Yellow Vests throw their weight behind mounting student protests</title><link>https://www.france24.com/en/france/20261017-live-france-s-yellow-vests-throw-their-weight-behind-mounting-student-protests</link><description>
Hundreds of thousands of ⁠people are expected to ​demonstrate across France on Saturday as students, trade union members and remnants of the Yellow Vest movement join forces to protest rising cost of living and ​the country's fraying social model. Follow our liveblog for the latest developments.
</description><media:thumbnail url="https://s.france24.com/media/display/e9533b5c-c9fa-11f1-8c76-2d1c143cdef3/w:1024/p:16x9/2026-10-17T070722Z-1548666842-RC2U4OA7SH8V-RTRMADP-3-FRANCE-PROTEST.jpg"/><enclosure url="https://s.france24.com/media/display/e9533b5c-c9fa-11f1-8c76-2d1c143cdef3/w:1024/p:16x9/2026-10-17T070722Z-1548666842-RC2U4OA7SH8V-RTRMADP-3-FRANCE-PROTEST.jpg" type="image/jpeg" length="0"/><guid isPermaLink="false">7ed0342a-c9e5-11f1-adfb-674a04d80b0a</guid><pubDate>Sat, 17 Oct 2026 05:17:22 GMT</pubDate><source url="https://s.france24.com/media/display/e9533b5c-c9fa-11f1-8c76-2d1c143cdef3/w:1024/p:16x9/2026-10-17T070722Z-1548666842-RC2U4OA7SH8V-RTRMADP-3-FRANCE-PROTEST.jpg">© Yann Tessier, Reuters</source><dc:creator>FRANCE 24</dc:creator></item><item><category>Europe</category><title>Zelensky turns to Europe for backing as ties with Trump deteriorate</title><link>https://www.france24.com/en/europe/20261016-zelensky-turns-to-europe-for-backing-as-ties-with-trump-deteriorate</link><description>
Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky turned to his European allies on Friday, asking Brussels for an additional €70 billion to fund the war against Russia next year. Zelensky's relationship with US President Donald Trump deteriorated after the US eased sanctions on Moscow as part of a diesel-supply deal.
</description><media:thumbnail url="https://s.france24.com/media/display/c6338998-c99a-11f1-9ea4-6313a763b466/w:1024/p:16x9/000-D3GY8H7.jpg"/><enclosure url="https://s.france24.com/media/display/c6338998-c99a-11f1-9ea4-6313a763b466/w:1024/p:16x9/000-D3GY8H7.jpg" type="image/jpeg" length="0"/><guid isPermaLink="false">c0dc235e-c99c-11f1-b230-09bd13f05fa4</guid><pubDate>Fri, 16 Oct 2026 20:25:46 GMT</pubDate><source url="https://s.france24.com/media/display/c6338998-c99a-11f1-9ea4-6313a763b466/w:1024/p:16x9/000-D3GY8H7.jpg">© Nicolas Tucat, AFP</source><dc:creator>FRANCE 24</dc:creator></item><item><category>Eye on Africa</category><title>KENYA CONFIRMS THIRD EBOLA CASE</title><link>https://www.france24.com/en/kenya-confirms-third-ebola-case</link><description>
In tonight's programme, Kenya confirms a third case of Ebola, a relative of a man who died earlier this month after travelling from DR Congo. Also,Cameroonian journalist Ambe Macmillan is recovering in hospital after being shot in the legs by gunmen in Bamenda. And we meet Ghanaian artist Ibrahim Mahama... And finally, we meet Ghanaian artist Ibrahim Mahama, who digs deep into his country's colonial and industrial past to lay new creative foundations for generations to come.
</description><media:thumbnail url="https://s.france24.com/media/display/a8234156-c99e-11f1-ac97-d1d2c32ebb87/w:1024/p:16x9/capture-d9ec4c85.jpg"/><enclosure url="https://s.france24.com/media/display/a8234156-c99e-11f1-ac97-d1d2c32ebb87/w:1024/p:16x9/capture-d9ec4c85.jpg" type="image/jpeg" length="0"/><guid isPermaLink="false">10ae7b4c-c99e-11f1-8421-dfc1b0a04897</guid><pubDate>Fri, 16 Oct 2026 20:25:16 GMT</pubDate><dc:creator>James MULHOLLAND</dc:creator></item><item><category>Europe</category><title>'Finish what we started': After student protests, France braces for return of the Yellow Vests</title><link>https://www.france24.com/en/europe/20261016-finish-what-we-started-after-student-protests-france-braces-return-yellow-vests</link><description>
An online movement against rising fuel prices has gained momentum ahead of planned nationwide demonstrations on October 17 with former Yellow Vest figures set to join the protests in support of high-school students. Some are drawing parallels between the latest action and the 2018 cost-of-living protests that rattled President Emmanuel Macron's first term in office.
</description><media:thumbnail url="https://s.france24.com/media/display/7a84b63e-c8a0-11f1-ac1f-638c1c1f5fd6/w:1024/p:16x9/000-1GD2EZ.jpg"/><enclosure url="https://s.france24.com/media/display/7a84b63e-c8a0-11f1-ac1f-638c1c1f5fd6/w:1024/p:16x9/000-1GD2EZ.jpg" type="image/jpeg" length="0"/><guid isPermaLink="false">97200a1c-c960-11f1-b0c0-219ae52178dc</guid><pubDate>Fri, 16 Oct 2026 20:10:18 GMT</pubDate><source url="https://s.france24.com/media/display/7a84b63e-c8a0-11f1-ac1f-638c1c1f5fd6/w:1024/p:16x9/000-1GD2EZ.jpg">© Jean-Philippe Ksiazek, AFP</source><dc:creator>Grégoire SAUVAGE</dc:creator></item></channel></rss>

      <description>China’s artificial intelligence companies have spent years persuading consumers to pay for their technology. Now, Moonshot AI, the start-up behind Kimi, is taking a different approach: offering AI computing benefits through a credit card.

      <description>For patients with advanced, metastatic cancer that has progressed despite systemic therapy – options remain critically limited.
Now, Chinese scientists are pointing to an unconventional therapeutic agent – the element iron.
This idea originated in industrial waste water treatment: iron can react with hydrogen peroxide to generate hydroxyl radicals, which degrade various organic and toxic molecules in waste water.
Chinese scientists wanted to treat malignant tumours the way they treat waste water...</description>

      <description>Many delegates to ⁠the International Monetary Fund’s steering ⁠committee walked out of a meeting on ⁠Saturday when Russian Finance Minister Anton Siluanov addressed the group in Russian, three sources familiar with the matter said.

      <description>Hong Kong police have received more than 100 reports of unauthorised credit card transactions related to pre-orders of Apple’s latest iPhone model, the South China Morning Post has learned.
Apple began its online pre-orders for its foldable iPhone Duo on Friday at 8pm, and complaints about suspicious transactions began to appear on social media overnight.
Some credit card users claimed duplicate or unauthorised purchases of the new model.
A source said the transactions involved a few million...</description>

      <description>Despite ⁠tens of thousands of security personnel deployed to stop them, youth protesters in India scaled barricades last ⁠week, chanted anti-government slogans and scuffled with police officers trying to drag them away.
“Long live the revolution,” shouted one young man before police bundled him into a bus.
Street protests in India this year are likely to be higher than at any time in the past decade, the independent Armed Conflict Location and Event Data Project has said, as dissent mounts...</description>

<![CDATA[ Latest from Space.com ]]> https://www.space.com/feeds.xml Fri, 16 Oct 2026 22:00:00 +0000 en <![CDATA[ 'It really does change you': SpaceX Crew-12 commander wishes we could all see our fragile Earth from space ]]> The astronauts of SpaceX's Crew-12 mission to the International Space Station wish that we could all see Earth as they just did.

An orbital view reveals the immense beauty of our blue planet, the only world we know of that hosts life. But it also highlights how fragile that life is, tethered to our lonely Earth in the vast void of space, according to Crew-12 commander Jessica Meir of NASA.

"You see this very thin, tenuous band of an atmosphere, and you know that that is all that is supporting life, and we really need to do our best to protect it," Meir said on Thursday afternoon (Oct. 15), during a press conference that discussed the recently concluded Crew-12 mission.

"I wish that I could bring all the eyes of all the humans to look back at the Earth in this extraordinary way that we are so privileged to have," she added. "I think it really does change you philosophically and [in] how you see each other, how you see yourself, how you see the human race when you look on it down from the vantage point that we have from above — you know, [it] gives everybody this understanding that we need to protect our planet, that it's not only so beautiful, but it's so precious."

From the International Space Station (ISS), Meir said, it's clear that everything on Earth is connected — and that the borders we've laid down between states and nations are artificial constructs.

"You realize that we really are one human when you are in space," she said. "I wish I could share that perspective with all the eyes of all the humans. I think it would be a very healthy thing for everyone to understand.

Crew-12 mission specialist Andrey Fedyaev, of the Russian space agency Roscosmos, voiced similar sentiments, though he would turn an ISS visitor's eyes inward, to focus on the crew.

"I always say that the life of crewmembers on board the space station is the best example of how people need to live on Earth," Fedyaev said during Thursday's briefing (in Russian; in interpreter translated his words into English in real time)."

"We don't have borders. We are all friendly. We're just one crew, and the safety of the crew, the safety of the station, depends on the actions of the entire crew," he added. "So, if humankind does arrive at the same conclusion — that our Earth, our planet, is one and the same space vessel that flies through space — we need to take care of it and not to destroy it. So, that's what I would like to show to everyone on Earth."

Meir and Fedyaev are far from the only ones to have their perpsectives shifted by a space mission. Pretty much every astronaut experiences this phenomenon, which is known as the overview effect, a term coined in 1987 by space philosopher Frank White.

Crew-12 consisted of Meir, Fedyaev, NASA astronaut Jack Hathaway (the mission's pilot) and the European Space Agency's Sophie Adenot (mission specialist). It was the second spaceflight for Meir and Fedyaev and the first for Hathaway and Adenot.

The quartet launched toward the ISS on Feb. 13 atop a SpaceX Falcon 9 rocket. Their Crew Dragon capsule, named Freedom, arrived at the orbiting lab a day later.

Crew-12 spent nearly eight months aboard the ISS, finally returning to Earth on Oct. 8. They conducted a wide range of scientific experiments and maintenance work during that time and set a few records as well.

For example, Adenot became the first French woman ever to perform a spacewalk, and she broke the mark for longest continuous spaceflight by a European at 237 days. The previous record, 201 days, was set by Luca Parmitano in 2019-2020.

]]> <![CDATA[ When not to watch a meteor shower — why I'm not staying up for the Orionids ]]> I used to think being interested in the night sky meant I had to try every meteor shower. If a calendar said "peak," I interpreted that as an instruction. I'd set an alarm, find several layers of clothing and go outside at around 2:00 a.m. when even the neighborhood cats seemed surprised to see me. Then I'd spend an increasingly resentful 45 minutes staring upward, occasionally see one meteor and wonder whether I was somehow doing it all wrong. As I've grown into stargazing, I've become much more selective.

The Orionids peak next week, and normally I'd be tempted. These fast meteors come from debris from Halley's Comet, which is enough of a connection to make almost anyone want to go outside. However, another object is in the sky this year — a big, bright waxing gibbous moon that will brighten the night sky and make "shooting stars" very hard to see.

That doesn't make the Orionids unobservable. In fact, there is a narrow window when the night sky will be free from moonlight. But it does make me far less inclined to sacrifice an entire night for them, and I certainly won't be trying to spend the night camping under a dark sky in a remote rural location far from light pollution. I've discovered that knowing when not to observe is an underrated stargazing skill.

What's happening and when to look

The Orionids are active from Oct. 2 through Nov. 7, with their 2026 maximum expected overnight on Oct. 21-22. They appear to radiate from a point near Orion, although the meteors themselves can streak across almost any part of the sky.

The shower happens because Earth crosses a stream of debris left behind by Halley's Comet, which was last in the inner solar system in 1986 and will return in 2061. Those tiny particles hit our atmosphere at roughly 41 miles (66 kilometers) per second, making Orionids particularly fast meteors.

Under ideal conditions, the International Meteor Organization gives the shower a zenithal hourly rate of 20 or more around maximum. But "zenithal hourly rate" is not the same as promising that I will personally see 20 meteors while standing in my backyard for an hour. It assumes an excellent dark sky, a well-placed radiant and unobstructed viewing. In reality, that's impossible — at the very least you'd have to have eyes in the back of your head. And on each side.

This year adds another complication. The moon reaches first quarter on Oct. 18 and continues waxing toward full on Oct. 26. On the peak night of the Orionids, an 80%-illuminated waxing gibbous moon will be in the night sky as it gets dark on Oct. 21 and sets around 03:00 a.m. local time across Europe and North America on Oct. 22. You can probably see the workaround. Sunrise is roughly 06:30 a.m. local time, which means astronomical darkness — when the sun is more than 18 degrees below the horizon, meaning complete darkness — lasts until around 05:00 a.m. local time (these times work as a ballpark, but you can (check the exact times of moonset and sunrise for your location on Time and Date).

So there is a dark window before dawn, and that is when I would try to see the shower if I were determined to see it. The Orionid radiant is also much better placed after midnight than it is in the evening.

Knowing exactly what's going to happen in the sky turns a casual meteor watch into a rather more calculated exercise.

How and when I'm watching it

My plan for the Orionids this year is the same as usual — after checking the moon phase and the moonset and sunrise times, there's one more variable. The weather forecast first.

If the forecast is excellent and I'm feeling enthusiastic, I'll target the period after moonset and before morning twilight on Oct. 22. If it's due to be cloudy, I'm staying in bed.

This sounds obvious, but I think beginners are sometimes given the impression that successful stargazing requires heroic commitment. It doesn't. A meteor shower is not a performance that disappears the moment the advertised "peak" passes. The Orionids have a relatively broad period of activity, so meteors can appear on nights either side of maximum, too.

If I do go outside at 3:00 a.m., I'll do so without two hugely valuable resources for meteor showers — a lawn chair and bags of patience.

Stargazer's corner: October 16-22, 2026

The moon reaches first quarter on Oct. 18, making stargazing tricky this week. That means I'm changing what I observe rather than declaring the week a write-off. The moon itself becomes an excellent target in early evening around first quarter. Sunlight strikes the lunar landscape along the terminator — the boundary between lunar day and night — throwing mountains and crater rims into strong relief. A cheap pair of binoculars can reveal a surprising amount. With a telescope, you can spend hours getting lost in the Montes Apenninus mountain range and three nearby craters — Eratosthenes and Archimedes on either side, and Plato above. Saturn remains another easy evening target after its Oct. 4 opposition. Look toward the eastern and southeastern sky after dark for its steady yellowish light. Even a modest telescope pointed at Saturn's rings will astound.

Constellation of the week: Cassiopeia

Cassiopeia is one of the easiest constellations I know to find because its five main stars form a conspicuous W — or, right now, something that looks suspiciously more like an M. Look toward the northern sky in the evening. From mid-northern latitudes, Cassiopeia is high and prominent during autumn, on the opposite side of Polaris from the Big Dipper. That relationship is more useful to me than memorizing exactly which way the W should point. Cassiopeia circles Polaris as Earth rotates, so its orientation changes through the night. From sufficiently northerly locations, it's circumpolar, meaning it never sets below the horizon.

The moon reaches first quarter on Oct. 18, making stargazing tricky this week. That means I'm changing what I observe rather than declaring the week a write-off. Sunlight strikes the lunar landscape along the terminator — the boundary between lunar day and night — throwing mountains and crater rims into strong relief. A cheap pair of binoculars can reveal a surprising amount. Saturn remains another easy evening target after its Oct. 4 opposition. Look toward the eastern and southeastern sky after dark for its steady yellowish light. Cassiopeia is one of the easiest constellations I know to find because its five main stars form a conspicuous W — or, right now, something that looks suspiciously more like an M. Look toward the northern sky in the evening. From mid-northern latitudes, Cassiopeia is high and prominent during autumn, on the opposite side of Polaris from the Big Dipper. From sufficiently northerly locations, it's circumpolar, meaning it never sets below the horizon.

]]> <![CDATA[ How to see the Orionid meteor shower 2026 peak this week — and when to look ]]> If you love watching meteors, 2026 has given you plenty to enjoy. This summer, the annual Perseid meteor shower peaked on the day of a new moon — and a solar eclipse — so moonlight stayed out of the way. And there's more to look forward to: in December, the Geminids, the year's most prolific shower, will peak after a waxing crescent moon sets early in the evening, opening the door to excellent viewing.

Right between those two headline showers, the dependable Orionids take their turn, reaching peak activity around Oct. 21-22.

So, when and where can you catch the show?

When and where to watch

The Orionids take their name from the spot where they seem to fan out: Orion's raised club, just above and to the left of the reddish star Betelgeuse. Orion is usually a winter favorite, so in early autumn the mighty hunter doesn't fully clear the eastern horizon until after 11 p.m. local daylight time. Don't rush outside just yet though. Wait until around 2 a.m., when Orion is well above the horizon. By about 5 a.m., just before dawn, Orion reaches its highest point in the southern sky — and the view should be at its best.

Orionid meteors tend to be faint, so city lights can easily wash them out. If you can, head to a safe, dark rural spot. Get comfortable in a reclining lawn chair or sleeping bag, give your eyes time to adjust, and enjoy the view overhead and toward the southern sky.

Why the moon won't spoil the show

And what about the moon? A full moon arrives October 25-26, but there's still a welcome stretch of dark sky for several mornings before Wednesday.

By Oct. 21-22, the waxing gibbous moon will be resting among the dim stars of Capricornus, reaching its highest point around 8:45 p.m. local daylight time. Here's the good news: it will set shortly after 2 a.m., leaving roughly 3½ hours of dark sky before dawn. In that window, one observer may spot as many as 15 to 20 Orionids per hour. Because those hours line up with the shower's peak, the moon shouldn't steal the show this year.

Halley's Comet: the source of the Orionids

So, where do the Orionids come from? Their story begins with Halley's Comet—the same famous visitor behind May's Eta Aquarids.

Meteoroids are tiny leftovers from a comet's nucleus. As a comet nears the sun, frozen material on its surface turns directly into gas, a process known as sublimation. The comet becomes a kind of cosmic litterbug, sprinkling dust and debris along its orbit. Those pieces are tiny and brittle, with the consistency of cigar ash, and every swing past the sun leaves more behind.

Comets are among the solar system's oldest and most fascinating objects. They formed alongside the sun and planets about 4.6 billion years ago, yet they have changed remarkably little. Think of them as time capsules from the solar system's childhood. Far beyond the outer planets, they spend most of their time in a deep freeze, where temperatures hover just above absolute zero, -459.67°F (-273.15°C). In that extreme cold, chemical reactions largely stop, helping comets preserve material from those earliest days.

Over the past 100,000 years, Halley's Comet has probably circled the sun well over a thousand times, leaving a fresh trail of debris on every visit. Each October and May, Earth brushes close to Halley's orbit. Some of that dust meets our atmosphere at a breathtaking 41 miles (66 km) per second, lighting up as the streaks we call "shooting stars."

The Orionids have another lovely feature: about half of these meteors leave glowing trails that linger longer than those of equally bright meteors. Halley's composition may be the reason. The particles begin burning up about 80 miles (130 km) above Earth, perhaps because they're made of lightweight material from the comet's diffuse surface rather than its core.

Looking backward . . . and forward

Perhaps you remember seeing Halley's Comet when it last swept through the inner solar system in late winter and early spring of 1986. With an orbital period of 75.4 years, this celebrated visitor is due back in late July or early August 2061.

For a little perspective, average life expectancy is 79.5 years in the United States, 82.2 years in the United Kingdom, and 83.4 years in Canada. So, if you were born after 1980, there's a fair chance you'll be here to welcome the "mother of all Orionids" home in 2061.

As for me, I saw Halley in 1986 at the "advanced age" of 30. The odds of another reunion are pretty long — you can do the math.

Until then, I'll be more than happy to step outside early on Wednesday morning and greet a few of "Halley's children." I hope you'll join me.

]]> <![CDATA[ Scientists find 'gemstones' in atmosphere of bizarre, scorching-hot 'marshmallow' exoplanet ]]> Using data from the James Webb Space Telescope (JWST), astronomers have unraveled some of the atmospheric secrets of a bizarre, blisteringly hot world that has the consistency of marshmallow.

The extrasolar planet, or exoplanet, under the watchful infrared eye of the JWST, is WASP-17b, located around 1,300 light-years away. The exoplanet has a mass around 0.8 times that of Jupiter, but it is around twice as wide as the solar system's largest planet, giving it a "super-puff" consistency comparable to the Earth-based treat. WASP-17 b is so close to its parent star that it completes an orbit in under four Earth days, with this proximity also making the temperature of this "hot Jupiter" skyrocket.

Given the extreme conditions of this exoplanet, it is little wonder that its atmosphere is pretty unusual too. Using a new technique called transmission strings, a team of scientists mapped the contours of the atmosphere of WASP-17b. They found that the atmosphere is shaped like a ring with prominent "gems" rising from it.

"Planets are temperamental, their atmospheres complex and chaotic," team member Hannah Wakeford of the University of Bristol said in a statement. "The fact that all of these numbers came together and showed us this very structured, dynamical picture of this giant world over 1,000 light-years away was just really exciting."

Astronomers like WASP-17b so much they put a ring on it

WASP-17b is so close to its parent star that it is tidally locked, meaning one side permanently faces the star; its dayside is constantly bombarded with stellar radiation. In contrast, the planet also has a cooler nightside, which faces out into space in perpetuity.

By creating incredibly comprehensive 3D views of this exoplanet's atmosphere, researchers found that WASP-17b's atmosphere has a chemical composition and temperature that shift between dayside and nightside according to theory and modelling.

This was possible because the transmission strings technique tracked WASP-17b as it crossed or transited in front of its star, capturing the composition of light around the edge of the planet's atmosphere, or limb, from different angles. This method trumps standard approaches because traditional modelling only maps light as an average across the entire limb.

"Rather than assuming your atmosphere is a circle with the same radius all the way around, our technique allows you to pull out different distances from the center to the edge of the planet," Lili Alderson, of Cornell University, said. "We're able to go around the edge.

"So, we've gone from a ring to understanding where on the ring the gemstones are, so to speak."

The modelling showed just such a "gem," that occurs where hot winds from the planet reach the equator and the nightside of WASP-17b, the atmosphere of the cooler side inflates.

"Theory predicts that the morning and the evening sides should have a strong temperature difference, and WASP-17b fits really nicely in that trend – pretty much bang-on what we thought it would be," Alderson said.

The successful application of the transmission strings method is an exciting step forward in the modelling of the atmospheres of the over 6,000 worlds in NASA's exoplanet catalog.

"This is proof of concept that planets are, in fact, 3D objects, and that, consistently, as they go around their star, what we predict should be happening is happening," Alderson concluded. "To move beyond computational exercises and see it for real is a different matter."

The team's research was published on Wednesday (Oct.14) in the journal Nature Astronomy.

]]> <![CDATA[ SpaceX thrusters just made a Tesla Roadster 'fly' (and Elon Musk's car is still out there in space) ]]>

Well, that was a memorable debut.

Tesla unveiled its highly anticipated new Roadster last night (Oct. 16) with a spectacular stunt, using SpaceX thrusters to make the vehicle "fly."

"This is not necessarily a safety-optimized car, OK?" Elon Musk, who runs both companies, said during the livestreamed reveal, which was held at SpaceX's rocket-testing facility in McGregor, Texas. "But it takes the the fun meter to 11 out of 10."

Tesla first announced the next-gen Roadster in 2017, saying at the time that it would be released in 2020. In 2018, Musk announced that the new car would incorporate some SpaceX tech.

"SpaceX option package for new Tesla Roadster will include ~10 small rocket thrusters arranged seamlessly around car. These rocket engines dramatically improve acceleration, top speed, braking & cornering. Maybe they will even allow a Tesla to fly…" he wrote on Twitter in June of that year. (In 2022, Musk bought Twitter, which he subsequently renamed X.)

So last night's demonstration didn't come entirely out of left field — but it was still eye-popping. The show began with the Roadster driving up a ramp that quickly became a vertical wall and then an overhanging ledge. The Roadster clung to the surface, hanging upside-down from the ledge like a gecko on a ceiling thanks to a special fan suction system on its chassis.

"I mean, this car really sucks, OK?" Musk said, channeling his inner stand-up comedian. "This car could suck the chrome off a trailer hitch. It could suck a tennis ball through a hose pipe."

The suction feature is not just a novelty, he added: It will help the Roadster stay connected to the ground during high-speed turns, allowing drivers to corner incredibly well.

And the sucking was just an opening act. The Tesla soon launched itself from its position beneath the ramp's nearly horizontal ledge, executed a barrel roll in midair, and landed softly, all thanks to its SpaceX cold-gas thrusters.

"A friend of mine, Peter Thiel, once said that the future promised us flying cars, but instead we got 140 characters," Musk said after the Roadster touched down. "Well, not anymore."

The car has main thrusters in the rear, he explained, as well as attitude-control thrusters that control its orientation.

"So it can basically fly like a rocket, and it could do rolls," Musk said. "It could do, like, crazy gymnastics — whatever you want, really."

The Roadster has a total of 10 thrusters, which are fed by 600 liters — about 250 kilograms (550 pounds) — of compressed air, Tesla Engineering Vice President Lars Moravy said during last night's event. That air is housed in carbon fiber overwrapped pressure vessels, which fill "every usable void in the car," Tesla said via X last night.

The Tesla team put those thrusters to work multiple times during the presentation, at one point launching the Roadster over a line of six vehicles, including a Tesla semi-truck cab.

Nobody was behind the wheel during these stunts — nobody with a pulse, anyway. The driver's seat was occupied by a mannequin clad in a black-and-white SpaceX spacesuit.

This was a nod to "Starman," the dummy behind the wheel of Musk's cherry-red first-gen Roadster, which launched into orbit around the sun in February 2018 on the first-ever flight of SpaceX's Falcon Heavy rocket.

Starman and his Roadster are still in space, by the way, and will be for a while. Modeling work suggests the duo will keep orbiting our star for millions of years before ultimately slamming into either Earth or Venus.

Last night's Roadster demo was something of a tease, for the car is not yet in showrooms. Musk said Tesla aims to begin producing it in 2028.

And don't expect to see the "flying" version on the road then, or anytime; it's hard to imagine regulators certifying that vehicle for everyday use. It will likely be a status symbol for a few wealthy and connected folks, locked away in spacious and well-appointed garages.

Indeed, you can't put down on a deposit for the "Rocket" version of the new Roadster on Tesla's website; purchase of that vehicle is by invite only.

Two other Roadster versions are for sale — "Performance" and "Thrust." Tesla's website describes the Performance variant as "road ready," with "active aero and a multi-mode suction system." Thrust, by contrast, is "race ready." It has active aero and suction "plus acceleration thrusters."

It costs $50,000 to reserve a Performance vehicle and $250,000 to reserve a Thrust. Tesla has not yet revealed the total cost of any of the new Roadster variants.

]]> <![CDATA[ On this day in space! Oct. 16, 1975: NASA launches the 1st-ever GOES weather satellite to watch Earth from space ]]>

On Oct. 16, 1975, NASA launched the first operational GOES satellite!

GOES-A was the first in a series of weather satellites that NASA jointly operated with the National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration (NOAA).

The name is short for Geostationary Operational Environmental Satellite. GOES-A launched on a Delta rocket from Cape Canaveral, Florida. GOES satellites all have a geostationary orbit, which means they always face the same part of Earth — in this case, the Indian Ocean. Once GOES-A became operational, it was renamed GOES-1.

The GOES satellite fleet has grown over the years, and is a critical link in the chain of satellites tracking Earth's weather from space. In 2016, NASA and NOAA launched GOES-R, the first in a new next-generation series of GOES weather satellites, with more to follow in ensuing years.

Why it mattered

With weather forecasts so prevalent (you can literally find them in the palm of your hand with a smartphone), it may be hard to think that such daily information wasn't always readily available. But that was the case when NOAA began building what has become an essential part of the U.S. weather monitoring fleet of satellites.

GOES-A, or GOES-1 as it was later called, "gave forecasters their first near-real time look at atmospheric conditions from a fixed location," NOAA officials said in an overview.

The satellite launched from Pad 17A at what is now the Cape Canaveral Space Force Station and returned its first photo just nine days after liftoff, on Oct. 25, 1975. The satellite was equipped with a Visible/Infrared Spin Scan Radiometer (VISSR) to capture Earth observations in daylight and nighttime to track clouds and surface temperature.

The spin-stabilized satellite was able to observe Earth just 10% of the time, but was still the most up-to-date satellite observations for weather forecasters.

GOES-1 was active until March 7, 1985, when it was ultimately decommissioned. But during that time, NASA and NOAA launched five more successors, GOES 2, 3, 4, 5 and 6.

"For 50 years, GOES data has been the backbone of short-term forecasts and warnings of severe weather and environmental hazards in the Western Hemisphere and forecasts and warnings of space weather hazards," NOAA wrote while celebrating 50 years of GOES satellites. "Each successive generation of GOES has brought improvements and new capabilities to monitor our part of the world."

Since the first next-generation GOES satellite, GOES-R, launched in 2016, NOAA has flown another three satellites, most recently with GOES-U weather satellite launch in 2024.

Want more space history? Check out our full On This Day In Space Story archive and watch our On This Day In Space videos on YouTube.

The name is short for Geostationary Operational Environmental Satellite. GOES-A launched on a Delta rocket from Cape Canaveral, Florida. GOES satellites all have a geostationary orbit, which means they always face the same part of Earth — in this case, the Indian Ocean. Once GOES-A became operational, it was renamed GOES-1.

The GOES satellite fleet has grown over the years, and is a critical link in the chain of satellites tracking Earth's weather from space. In 2016, NASA and NOAA launched GOES-R, the first in a new next-generation series of GOES weather satellites, with more to follow in ensuing years.

Why it mattered

With weather forecasts so prevalent (you can literally find them in the palm of your hand with a smartphone), it may be hard to think that such daily information wasn't always readily available. But that was the case when NOAA began building what has become an essential part of the U.S. weather monitoring fleet of satellites.

GOES-A, or GOES-1 as it was later called, "gave forecasters their first near-real time look at atmospheric conditions from a fixed location," NOAA officials said in an overview.

The satellite launched from Pad 17A at what is now the Cape Canaveral Space Force Station and returned its first photo just nine days after liftoff, on Oct. 25, 1975. The satellite was equipped with a Visible/Infrared Spin Scan Radiometer (VISSR) to capture Earth observations in daylight and nighttime to track clouds and surface temperature.

The spin-stabilized satellite was able to observe Earth just 10% of the time, but was still the most up-to-date satellite observations for weather forecasters.

GOES-1 was active until March 7, 1985, when it was ultimately decommissioned. But during that time, NASA and NOAA launched five more successors, GOES 2, 3, 4, 5 and 6.

"For 50 years, GOES data has been the backbone of short-term forecasts and warnings of severe weather and environmental hazards in the Western Hemisphere and forecasts and warnings of space weather hazards," NOAA wrote while celebrating 50 years of GOES satellites. "Each successive generation of GOES has brought improvements and new capabilities to monitor our part of the world."

Since the first next-generation GOES satellite, GOES-R, launched in 2016, NOAA has flown another three satellites, most recently with GOES-U weather satellite launch in 2024.

For Edgerton and Connelly, "Dark Matter" has been a whirlwind project as their characters search for a safe alternate universe while being pursued by a multiplicity of Jasons. The physical rigors and emotional toll of shooting the show and presenting its nuanced storytelling often proved difficult.

"There's two exhaustions that I’ve found in movie work," Edgerton tells Space. "It's either mental exhaustion from going to dark emotional places in your brain or complex dialogue stuff. Then there's the physical challenges, like for doing a fight scene. One of the weirdest ones on 'Dark Matter' was doing a gravity scene where we’re dangling on wires inside The Box. There's something deeply exhausting about it and a bit humiliating. You feel like a human teabag."

Connelly was also a part of that tough sequence and reflects on Edgerton’s tireless fortitude.

"Joel's schedule on this show is really brutal," she notes. "He's in almost all of it. This season is better, but season 1 was crazy for him. It’s surprising; sometimes the things that are most difficult are the ones you don’t anticipate. That's more exhausting at the end of the day after trying to get something to work that you didn’t think would be tricky. I like the days that are tiring because you feel drained because you’ve explored a lot in a scene. That's a nice feeling."

For Edgerton, the simplest thing to remember is that when practicing your craft, always make sure that you go home each day feeling satisfied with what you shot.

"There's nothing worse than going home and thinking that you didn’t get the best out of yourself," he reveals. "As they say, as actors we're not digging trenches. It's not hard physical labor; it's a different kind of thing. Until actually I shot a movie where I had to dig a trench."

Working with Blake Crouch on the series and its unnerving portrait of a marriage strewn across the infinite multiverse has produced new insights into their own lives.

"I find there’s something to be learned from each experience as an actor," notes Edgerton. "Each story takes you through something, whether you like to think it or not.

"You either learn a skill or meet an actor that you admire, and they teach you something inspired by their presence. We were tasked with helping Blake build the disintegration of a marriage, and it's the opposite of what you’re hoping for in real life. That each day you hope you're turning up contributing in a positive way to your relationship rather than engineering its demise. It makes you think about how you can be a better person in life. And there's always room for improvement."

Likewise, Connelly sees a sort of emotional mirroring effect to be absorbed that extends beyond "Dark Matter's" detailed sets, dizzying locations, and sound stages.

"I think Daniela, at a point when Jason is going down paths, and they're struggling, recognizes that sometimes it's hard to distinguish what is really the other person and what we’re bringing to our perception of them," she adds.

"She has things in her history that bias her vision, and she takes herself off on a journey to reconcile those things and try to take responsibility for healing. And that's a good lesson to remember in relationships in general. Being on top of one's own part of the dynamic. Sometimes things we see in each other are really things within ourselves."

]]> <![CDATA[ 'Mission: 60s' event promises passport back to the Space Age ]]> Your invitation to revisit the Space Age has arrived.

Whether you miss the days when people got dressed up to fly or you wish your "other" ride was a rocket, Mission: 60s has a *space* reserved for you.

"This is a three-day celebration of Apollo, aviation, space exploration and 1960s culture," reads a promo for the Oct. 23 to 25 event in New York. "You will be fully immersed in the sights, sounds and spirit of the 1960s Space Age."

"The weekend features astronauts, Apollo flight directors, Mission Control engineers, Star Trek legends, space artists, a Saturday Spacefarer Soiree with live music (1960s attire encouraged!), and a Sunday NASA Artemis keynote."

Organized by Luna Replicas, a company specializing in vintage space gear, and Space for Humanity, a nonprofit that underwrites spaceflight experiences, Mission: 60s is aimed at being the bridge between the last time humanity reached for the moon and today's "second space race" to do it again — this time to stay.

Launch pad

Your journey back to the 60s begins when you check into the TWA Hotel at the John F. Kennedy International Airport (JFK) in New York.

Once a functioning terminal for Trans World Airlines (as featured in the 2002 movie "Catch Me If You Can"), the TWA Flight Center has been reimagined as a hotel like no other.

"At the center of the hotel is Eero Saarinen's iconic TWA Flight Center, where restaurants, bars and retail outlets have taken flight. Two hotel wings, designed to reflect and defer to the landmark TWA Flight Center, sit behind the historic building and contain 512 guest rooms with views of JFK's runways and the TWA Flight Center," reads the hotel's website.

The TWA Hotel is only the first sight straight out of the past that guests will encounter. On Friday (Oct. 23), Mission: 60s begins with a guided tour of the 1964 World's Fair site in Flushing Meadows. Today the home to the New York Hall of Science, the outdoor exhibits includes the Rocket Park, where Gemini-Titan II and Mercury-Atlas D rockets and a Saturn V F-1 engine still stand.

"The space age was less than 10 years old when rockets like these powered incredible missions to outer space," reads the description on the museum's website. "Visitors will learn about the history of these vehicles as well as the United States' mission to reach the moon."

Also on view at the World's Fair site is the Unisphere, a spherical stainless steel representation of Earth, and the Astro-View Observation Towers (later reimagined as actual flying saucers in the 1997 movie "Men in Black").

The first day concludes with Space For Humanity's (separately-ticketed) "Celestial Soiree" and a Mission: 60's pool party on the hotel's rooftop.

MCC, ILC and ILM

Saturday and Sunday at Mission: 60s will bring together members of Mission Control (MCC), spaceflight experts (including ILC Dover, makers of the Apollo spacesuit) and representatives from the Hollywood community who brought about the 60s-era visions of space exploration (including Industrial Light & Magic [ILM]) for a series of engaging panel discussions.

Among the various topics scheduled for the two days of talks are:

  • Apollo Mission Control & Flight Operations
  • Apollo to Artemis & Beyond
  • Women in Aerospace
  • Apollo Communications: The Sights & Sounds From the Moon
  • SciFi Inspires
  • The Overview Effect
  • Making Space Real: Art & Visual Effects That Sold Humanity on Space
  • Space Advocacy

Featured speakers and moderators include Apollo flight director Gerry Griffin, TIME Magazine science editor Jeffrey Kluger, former NASA astronauts Nicole Stott and Ron Garan, "Star Trek" actor Bob Picardo and researcher Frank White.

On Saturday evening, there will be a second gala, "The Spacefarer Soiree," featuring a limited meet and greet aboard a Lockheed Constellation airliner and music by Bonnie Gordon. Set in 1969, attendees are encouraged to come wearing their finest period clothing.

Then, on Sunday afternoon, Uplift Aerospace will host a shared "Overview" VR experience for up to 50 people participating together.

Both days will include a vendor and artists' hall, with guests signing autographs and their books, as well as companies such as NASA's official patch provider A-B Emblem, selling Apollo-themed souvenirs and memorabilia.

A weekend pass is $150 per person, with add-ons for VIP access, the galas and Friday's World Fair excursion. Single-day admission is $85.

]]> <![CDATA[ Why can you see the moon during the day? This week is the perfect time to find out ]]> I know perfectly well that the moon comes out during the day. I have known this for decades. Yet whenever I spot it in a blue afternoon sky, some primitive part of my brain still thinks it has turned up early.

I'm certainly not the only one. Many people don't understand how it could be visible in daylight. In their eyes, the moon is a nighttime object. Why? Because that's when they notice it — it appears brighter.

We tend to think of the sun as belonging to the day and the moon to the night because that's how they're usually presented to us as children. Astronomically, it makes little sense. The moon spends plenty of time above our horizon while the sun is also up — it spends half its time in the daytime sky, in fact.

If the moon, pale but unmistakable, looks slightly out of place against a blue sky, it's not — you are. This week is a great time to get used to seeing it there. Just past first quarter, the moon will spend each afternoon hanging in the daytime sky, becoming easier to spot as the sun sinks towards the horizon.

What's happening and when to look

The moon reached first quarter on Sunday, Oct. 18, and is now waxing toward full moon, which occurs early on Monday, Oct. 26 (Oct. 25 in some time zones). That puts it in the right part of its orbit to be conspicuous during the late afternoon this weekend.

Here's the useful bit to remember. Around first quarter, the moon rises roughly around midday. As it waxes towards full, it rises progressively later in the afternoon. By full moon, it rises around sunset.

That makes the days immediately after first quarter an excellent time to get into the habit of finding the moon before sunset. On Monday, Oct. 19, look southeast in the afternoon for a moon just over half-lit. Each afternoon this week, it will become a little more illuminated, move farther east against the background stars, and appear progressively later in the day.

You don't need to wait until dusk. In fact, that's the point. Start looking during the afternoon, when the sun is still well above the horizon. Once you find the moon, it can be surprisingly conspicuous against the blue sky.

How and when I'm watching it

I'll start looking in the mid-to-late afternoon this week, when the waxing moon should already be high enough to find easily. You can check the exact moonrise time where you are, but there's no need to catch it as it rises. Look towards the east or southeast and scan the blue sky.

Once you've found the moon in daylight, keep checking on it as sunset approaches. The moon doesn't suddenly become brighter, of course. Instead, the surrounding sky darkens, increasing the contrast until the pale daytime moon seems to switch on at dusk and grow increasingly brilliant.

Binoculars will give you a superb view at dusk, particularly along the terminator — the boundary between lunar day and night. That's where low-angle sunlight throws mountains and crater rims into sharp relief. As the moon waxes this week, the terminator will move steadily across its surface, revealing a different landscape each afternoon.

That's another reason not to wait for the full moon. The full moon gets most of the attention, but the week beforehand is arguably a much better time to get to know our nearest celestial neighbor — and you don't even have to wait until dark.

Stargazer's corner: October 23-29, 2026

This is a bright-moon week. Full moon arrives early on Monday, Oct. 26, so moonlight will wash out faint stars and make galaxies and nebulas much harder to see. So go for Saturn instead. It reached opposition earlier this month and remains very well placed in the evening sky. Better still, the nearly full moon passes near Saturn around Oct. 23-24, giving beginners a convenient landmark for locating the planet. The moon's glare will hide faint nearby stars, but Saturn itself is easily bright enough to cope. A good example will be Oct. 27, when the Pleiades is passed closely by a bright moon. The Seven Sisters therefore won't be at their best, so you'll need to use binoculars — if you do, you'll see them easily enough.

Constellation of the week: Auriga

Auriga, "the Charioteer," is climbing in the northeastern and eastern sky during late October evenings. It's easiest to find if you start at Capella, one of the brightest stars in the entire night sky. It's just 43 light-years from the sun. From there, I look for the other stars that form Auriga's rough pentagon, including Menkalinan, Mahasim and Almaaz. The fifth corner is Elnath, although it officially belongs to neighboring Taurus.

Auriga gets even better with binoculars. The Milky Way runs straight through it, bringing with it three bright open star clusters — M36, M37 and M38. All three show up in binoculars under a reasonably dark sky, while a small telescope starts to resolve them into individual stars. There's always another layer to find in the night sky.

My latest stargazing obsession

There's something special about stargazing during the blue hour — that brief transition when daylight drains from the sky and night's window begins to open. It's particularly beautiful a few days before full moon, when the near-full orb is already rising in the east as the sun sets in the west. Look below it, and you may also see the Belt of Venus, a pinkish band above the eastern horizon caused by reddened sunlight shining through Earth's atmosphere, with our planet's dark blue-gray shadow beneath. As the sky fades through ever-deeper shades of blue, the moon brightens, and the first stars emerge around it.

]]> <![CDATA[ 7 best places to see the northern lights, according to an aurora chaser ]]> I've spent years chasing the northern lights across the Arctic, from the mountains of Swedish Lapland to the dramatic Norwegian fjords.

If there's one thing I've learned, it's that choosing where to see the northern lights is about much more than simply heading as far north as possible. Whether you're on the hunt for somewhere that offers the best chance of clear skies, the most dramatic scenery or a plethora of winter activities to keep you warm, choosing the right destination can make a big difference, especially as auroras are never guaranteed.

My biggest piece of advice? Choose somewhere you've always wanted to visit regardless of whether the northern lights might appear. That way, the auroras become the icing on the cake rather than the sole measure of a successful trip.

From my personal favorites in Scandinavia to some of North America's most established aurora hotspots, here are seven of the best places to see the northern lights this 2026/27 season.

Abisko and Kiruna, Sweden: Best for a short northern lights trip

Best time to visit: September to early April

Swedish Lapland holds a particularly special place in my heart. It's where I saw the northern lights for the very first time, during a trip to Kiruna in February 2023.

 <description>Terezínská historická stavidla z 18. století se dočkají opravy. Město už vybralo firmu, která se do rekonstrukce evropského technického unikátu pustí. Radnice stavidla nadřadila některým větším opravám terezínských památek z vládního programu. Podle nezávislého starosty Reného Tomáška jsou totiž v havarijním stavu.</description>

 <description>Cestující na pražském Smíchovském nádraží čeká od úterý změna. Do vlaků budou nastupovat ze dvou nových nástupišť a dostanou se na ně jen přestavěným a prodlouženým podchodem. Železničáři kromě úpravy nástupišť staví také novou lávku do Radlic. </description>

<item>
 <title>Ekologická péče pro krávy v Doupovských horách. V areálu se o ně stará robot, provoz se řídí zdálky online</title>
 <link>https://www.irozhlas.cz/zpravy-domov/ekologicka-pece-pro-kravy-v-doupovskych-horach-v-arealu-se-o-ne-stara-robot_2610170600_brz</link>
 <description>Vojenské lesy a statky otevřely v Javorné v Doupovských horách nový areál pro ekologický chov skotu. Zimovištěm projde každý rok přes 200 mladých jalovic a ve stáji poprvé nasadí robota, který se postará o jejich podestýlání. Zvířata budou mít volný přístup na okolní pastviny a provoz areálu bude možné sledovat a řídit na dálku prostřednictvím bezdrátového připojení.</description>

<item>
 <title>ONLINE: Druhé kolo voleb do Senátu je bez větších problémů. Kandidáty mohou lidé vybírat do 14 hodin</title>
 <link>https://www.irozhlas.cz/zpravy-domov/online-lide-znovu-voli-rozhodnou-o-zbyvajicich-22-senatorech-mistnosti-se_2610170605_med</link>
 <description>V Česku pokračuje druhé kolo senátních voleb. V sobotu se volební místnosti znovu otevřely v 8 hodin ráno, lidé mají čas odevzdat svůj hlas do 14 hodin. Rozhodnou o obsazení zbývajících 22 senátorských křesel. Pět kandidátů uspělo už v prvním kole minulý týden. O výsledcích jednotlivých soubojů by mělo být jasno během sobotního odpoledne.</description>

   <title>Výplaty důchodů se změní. O peníze ale nepřijdete, uklidňují experti</title>
   <link>https://www.denik.cz/ekonomika/cesko-duchody-vyplaty-penzi-se-zmeni/?utm_source=rss&utm_medium=feed-vse&utm_campaign=ceskolipsky.denik.cz&utm_content=ekonomika</link>
   <description>Systém výplaty důchodů v Česku projde příští rok zásadní změnou. Místo dosavadního klouzavého období se penze budou vyplácet za kalendářní měsíc, což má zjednodušit orientaci téměř třem milionům příjemců. Změna eliminuje situace, kdy lednová výplata působí vyšší než únorová, což dosud vyvolávalo nejasnosti ohledně správné výše valorizovaného důchodu.</description>
   <pubDate>Sat, 17 Oct 2026 04:00:00 +0200</pubDate>
   <guid>https://www.denik.cz/ekonomika/cesko-duchody-vyplaty-penzi-se-zmeni/</guid>

   <media:content url="https://ceskolipsky.denik.cz/images/api/image/1366x768/829/8293b3e7-a7e9-4bce-8dd5-79022e161b02.jpeg" medium="image" height="768" width="1366">
    <media:description>Důchodový systém zohledňuje celou pracovní historii, nikoli jen poslední výplatní pásku. Výslednou částku proto ovlivňuje kombinace výdělků, délky pojištění a pravidel platných pro konkrétní rok odchodu do důchodu.</media:description>

   <title>Třinec po první ztrátě znovu vítězí. Mazanec i Kořenář vynulovali soupeře</title>
   <link>https://www.denik.cz/hokej/extraliga-ouhrn-vysledky-trinec-boleslal-plzen-sparta-kladno-brno/?utm_source=rss&utm_medium=feed-vse&utm_campaign=ceskolipsky.denik.cz&utm_content=hokej</link>
   <description>Vedoucí Třinec po rekordním vstupu do hokejové extraligy minule ztratil první body v sezoně v Pardubicích, doma se ale hned vrátil zpátky na vítěznou vlnu.    <link>https://ceskolipsky.denik.cz/volny-cas/recenze-knihy-dobyti-rise-inku-tazeni-francisca-pizarra-v-letech-1532-1537/?utm_source=rss&utm_medium=feed-vse&utm_campaign=ceskolipsky.denik.cz&utm_content=volny-cas</link>

      <title>NKÚ nabere 16 nových zaměstnanců kvůli ostraze budovy. O policejní ochranu přišel</title>
      <link>https://www.idnes.cz/zpravy/domaci/nku-nejvyssi-kontrolni-urad-zamestanci-ochrana-budova-policie.A261017_084146_domaci_ikro#utm_source=rss&utm_medium=feed&utm_campaign=zpravodaj&utm_content=main</link>
      <description>Nejvyšší kontrolní úřad (NKÚ) zřídí od příštího roku kvůli ostraze svého sídla 16 nových pracovních míst. Půjde o 15 míst pro pracovníky ochrany budovy a jedno místo jejich vedoucího. Příslušnou změnu platového řádu, která to umožní, schválil v pondělí sněmovní rozpočtový výbor. Mluvčí NKÚ Hana Kadečková sdělila, že peníze na nové lidi úřad vyčleněné nemá a bude je muset vzít z provozních výdajů.</description>

<link>https://www.lupa.cz/aktuality/jednotne-mesicni-hlaseni-zamestnavatele-se-stat-chysta-rozsirit-o-dalsi-udaje-navrhuje-i-dosud-nefungujici-sdileni/?utm_source=rss&utm_medium=text&utm_campaign=rss</link>
<description>Jednotné měsíční hlá&#353;ení zaměstnavatele (JMHZ) má státu umožnit sbírat dal&#353;í údaje o zaměstnancích a zpřístupnit je více úřadům. Ministerstvo práce a sociálních věcí navrhuje změny, které mají reagovat na novou legislativu i praktické potřeby státních institucí. K návrhu přibyly nové dokumenty v oficiálním systému ODok.</description>

<description>Někdej&#353;í internetový fenomén hromadných slev Groupon, který kormidlují Če&#353;i z Pale Fire Capial, se otevřel obchodování, při kterém si zážitky nemají kupovat lidé, ale dělat to za ně mají AI agenti. <item>
<title>Česko pomáhá rozhýbat evropský čipový průmysl. Nová služba vývojářům ušetří hromadu práce</title>
<link>https://www.lupa.cz/aktuality/cesko-pomaha-rozhybat-evropsky-cipovy-prumysl-nova-sluzba-vyvojarum-usetri-hromadu-prace/?utm_source=rss&utm_medium=text&utm_campaign=rss</link>
<description>Český národní polovodičový klastr ve spolupráci s Českým polovodičovým centrem vytvořily užitečný online nástroj. Jde o katalog takzvaných IP bloků používaných při vývoji čipů. Tyto bloky v katalogu nabízí firmy a organizace z Evropy. Cílem je polovodičovým návrhářům nabídnout jednoduchý přístup ke klíčovým technologiím, které jsou ověřené a rychle nasaditelné a není je nutné vynalézat znovu.</description>

<title>Miliarda jim trvala tři roky, druhá jen pět měsíců. Českou AI naději už používají Meta, Xiaomi nebo Nvidia</title>

<description>Český startup E2B aktuálně patří k největ&#353;ím technologickým nadějím země.  <link>https://www.irozhlas.cz/zpravy-svet/s-pozarem-na-jihu-kalifornie-ktery-siri-silny-vitr-bojuji-stovky-hasicu-16-tisic_2610170814_bva</link>
 <description>Rychle se šířící požár rozdmýchávaný silným větrem zničil v okrese Orange na jihu Kalifornie nejméně šest domů. Úřady nařídily evakuaci 16 000 obyvatel. Kvůli požáru byly přerušeny dodávky elektřiny desetitisícům lidí, píše agentura AP.</description>

<item>
 <title>ONLINE: Trump pozastavil nový balík protiruských sankcí. ‚Je to v národním zájmu USA,‘ uvedl</title>
 <link>https://www.irozhlas.cz/zpravy-svet/online-trump-pozastavil-novy-balik-protiruskych-sankci-je-v-narodnim-zajmu-usa_2610170645_bva</link>
 <description>Americký prezident Donald Trump v pátek podepsal exekutivní příkaz, kterým pozastavuje uplatňování nového rozsáhlého balíku sankcí namířených proti ruské ekonomice. Kongresu sdělil, že je to v národním zájmu Spojených států, píše agentura AP. Zákon umožňující prezidentovi zavést rozsáhlé sankce, které mají dostat Rusko pod větší tlak a napomoci ukončení války na Ukrajině, schválila minulý měsíc Sněmovna reprezentantů a Trump ho posléze podepsal.</description>

</item>
<item>
 <title>Francii čeká v sobotu další protest středoškoláků. ‚Půjdou vyjádřit své zoufalství,‘ říká studentka</title>
 <link>https://www.irozhlas.cz/zpravy-svet/francii-ceka-v-sobotu-dalsi-protest-stredoskolaku-pujdou-vyjadrit-sve-zoufalstvi_2610162237_kma</link>
 <description>Francouzská vláda se od začátku října potýká s masovými protesty studujících, kteří napříč zemí blokují ulice a školy kvůli nedostatkům ve vzdělávání – další protest čeká Francii už v sobotu. „Francouzi se sejdou na podporu středoškoláků, ale nejvíc také proto, abychom jedním hlasem vyjádřili naše zoufalství nad nemožností něco změnit,“ říká pro redakci iROZHLAS.cz vysokoškolačka Romane Quenehenová.</description>
 <enclosure url="https://www.irozhlas.cz/sites/default/files/styles/zpravy_maly_nahled/public/uploader/2026-10-14t000000z_4_261016-215944_kma.JPG?itok=lK1QTS7A" type="image/jpeg" />

</item>
<item>
 <title>Smetana: USA přes Starlink tlačí na Ukrajinu. Časem ho mohou nahradit evropské družice</title>
 <link>https://www.irozhlas.cz/zpravy-svet/smetana-usa-pres-starlink-tlaci-na-ukrajinu-casem-ho-na-ukrajine-mohou-nahradit_2610162102_kma</link>
 <description>Ukrajinský prezident Volodymyr Zelenskyj cítí od Evropy plnou podporu, kontinent je podle něj velmi sjednocen, řekl v pátek po jednání v Bruselu. Na druhou stranu agentura Reuters napsala, že pokyn ke zpomalení Starshieldu na Ukrajině vydal přímo Bílý dům. „V rámci širší politické dynamiky je to určitý nátlak,“ říká Michal Smetana, bezpečnostní expert z Fakulty sociálních věd Univerzity Karlovy a ředitel Centra pro výzkum míru.</description>

 <description>Americký prezident Donald Trump v pátek prohlásil, že on ani miliardář Elon Musk nemohou za výpadek služby satelitní sítě Starlink na ukrajinské straně, píše Reuters. <item>

 <link>https://www.irozhlas.cz/zpravy-svet/trump-naznacil-ze-jeho-nova-mluvci-konci-zachariaova-byla-ve-funkci-tyden_2610162012_jkd</link>
 <description>Prezident Donald Trump v pátek naznačil, že jeho nová mluvčí Katie Zachariaová ve funkci brzy skončí. Konečné rozhodnutí šéf Bílého domu oznámí později, píše AP. Šéf tiskového odboru Bílého domu Steven Cheung později uvedl, že Zachariaová se přesune do nové funkce, která bude oznámena později, napsal v pátek večer deník The New York Times.</description>

</item>
<item>
 <title>Trumpovy Spojené státy musí prohrát. Je na Evropě, aby to bylo co nejrychleji, apeluje Lech Wałęsa</title>
 <link>https://www.irozhlas.cz/zpravy-svet/trumpovy-spojene-staty-musi-prohrat-evropa-se-musi-snazit-aby-bylo-co_2610161913_kvr</link>
 <description>Legendární odborářský lídr a bývalý polský prezident Lech Wałęsa byl svědkem přelomových událostí 20. století. Jak se dívá na dnešní svět? Evropa podle něj potřebuje novou vizi, zároveň varuje před důsledky politiky Donalda Trumpa. „Trump musí prohrát. Nemá žádnou šanci, protože postupuje v rozporu s vývojem světa. My bychom měli přemýšlet, jak omezit škody, které utrpíme,“ říká v Interview Plus.</description>

</item>

 <link>https://www.irozhlas.cz/zpravy-svet/trump-nechce-prohrat-midterms-sankce-na-ruskou-naftu-pozastavil-ze-sobeckych_2610161755_med</link>
 <description>„Systémovou, dlouhodobou a loajální pomoc svému spojenci vyměnil za krátkodobé politické cíle v řádu několika týdnů,“ komentuje rozhodnutí amerického prezidenta Donalda Trumpa pozastavit sankce na ruskou naftu odborník na mezinárodní vztahy a bezpečnost Vlastislav Bříza. Blíží se definitivní konec americké pomoci Ukrajině?</description>

 <link>https://www.irozhlas.cz/zpravy-svet/je-lepsi-se-nicim-nechlubit-kdyz-se-neco-podari-opravit-zautoci-dalsi-drony-rika_2610161329_med</link>
 <description>Rusko dále pokračuje v intenzivních útocích na Kyjev. „Snažíme se žít normálně, ale je to iluze. Od konce srpna jsou slyšet výbuchy prakticky každou hodinu a k tomu se přidala nová taktika balistických útoků. Lidé ztrácejí možnost včas se ukrýt a ve městě jsou každý den civilní oběti,“ popisuje právnička Katja Andrejevová žijící v Kyjevě.</description>

 <link>https://www.irozhlas.cz/zpravy-svet/kdo-prosazuje-ets2-prohraje-volby-vzkazal-babis-na-summitu-v4-zada-nove_2610161241_kch</link>
 <description>Několika členským státům Evropské unie včetně Česka se do závěrů summitu EU podařilo dostat novou výzvu Evropské komisi, aby znovu vyhodnotila dopady systému emisních povolenek ETS2. Vyplývá to ze závěrů prvního dne jednání, který proběhl ve čtvrtek. Evropská rada rovněž nově výslovně zdůraznila, že v rámci přezkumu systému ETS je třeba omezit kolísání cen emisních povolenek a zmírnit jejich dopad na ceny elektřiny.</description>

<description>Někdej&#353;í internetový fenomén hromadných slev Groupon, který kormidlují Če&#353;i z Pale Fire Capial, se otevřel obchodování, při kterém si zážitky nemají kupovat lidé, ale dělat to za ně mají AI agenti. <description>Český národní polovodičový klastr ve spolupráci s Českým polovodičovým centrem vytvořily užitečný online nástroj. Jde o katalog takzvaných IP bloků používaných při vývoji čipů. Tyto bloky v katalogu nabízí firmy a organizace z Evropy. Cílem je polovodičovým návrhářům nabídnout jednoduchý přístup ke klíčovým technologiím, které jsou ověřené a rychle nasaditelné a není je nutné vynalézat znovu.</description>

Po titulu mistryně Evropy v závodech Spartan ovládla také sprint na světovém šampionátu v chorvatském Hvaru.</description></item><item><title>Zažijte magický sklářský víkend. Vyrazte za zážitkem a vyrobte si třeba vlastní šperk.</description></item><item><title>Přechod, kde si chodci rozsvítí zelenou sami, navrhl pro Zálesní Lhotu student</title><link>https://liberecka.drbna.cz/doprava/902954-prechod-kde-si-chodci-rozsviti-zelenou-sami-navrhl-pro-zalesni-lhotu-student.html</link><guid isPermaLink="true">https://liberecka.drbna.cz/doprava/902954-prechod-kde-si-chodci-rozsviti-zelenou-sami-navrhl-pro-zalesni-lhotu-student.html</guid><pubDate>Fri, 16 Oct 2026 19:53:00 +0200</pubDate><category>Doprava</category><description>V Zálesní Lhotě na Semilsku slouží od srpna nový přechod se semaforem, který si chodci spouštějí tlačítkem. Navrhl ho student a jeho nápad se proměnil ve skutečné dopravní opatření. Přechod řeší dlouholetý problém na frekventované silnici, kterou denně přecházejí i děti cestou na autobus.</description></item><item><title>Končící starosta Ralska Miloslav Tůma do Sněmovny za Jitku Volfovou nenastoupí</title><link>https://liberecka.drbna.cz/politika/903158-koncici-starosta-ralska-miloslav-tuma-do-snemovny-za-jitku-volfovou.html</link><guid isPermaLink="true">https://liberecka.drbna.cz/politika/903158-koncici-starosta-ralska-miloslav-tuma-do-snemovny-za-jitku-volfovou.html</guid><pubDate>Fri, 16 Oct 2026 18:12:00 +0200</pubDate><dc:creator>ČTK</dc:creator><category>Politika</category><description>Končící starosta Ralska Miloslav Tůma (ANO) se rozhodl po 12 letech opustit politiku, vzdát se mandátu zastupitele v Ralsku a nenastoupí ani do Poslanecké sněmovny v případě, že jeho stranickou kolegyni, dosluhující starostku České Lípy Jitku Volfovou zvolí ve druhém kole do Senátu.</description></item><item><title>Užijte si v sobotu Den se železnicí na Liberecku, nabídne bohatý program</title><link>https://liberecka.drbna.cz/doprava/903197-uzijte-si-v-sobotu-den-se-zeleznici-na-liberecku-nabidne-bohaty-program.html</link><guid isPermaLink="true">https://liberecka.drbna.cz/doprava/903197-uzijte-si-v-sobotu-den-se-zeleznici-na-liberecku-nabidne-bohaty-program.html</guid><pubDate>Fri, 16 Oct 2026 16:00:00 +0200</pubDate><dc:creator>Martina Petrášková</dc:creator><category>Doprava</category><description>Chcete se v jednom dni na jednom místě setkat se staršími i moderními vozidly ve flotile Českých drah? Pak byste v sobotu 17. října neměli chybět v Liberci. České dráhy (ČD) na tento den připravily Den se železnicí na Liberecku, který nabídne nezapomenutelné zážitky pro malé i velké.</description></item><item><title>Souboj o Senát na Českolipsku. Rozhodne se mezi hejtmanem a starostkou Lípy</title><link>https://liberecka.drbna.cz/politika/903179-souboj-o-senat-na-ceskolipsku-rozhodne-se-mezi-hejtmanem-a-starostkou-lipy.html</link><guid isPermaLink="true">https://liberecka.drbna.cz/politika/903179-souboj-o-senat-na-ceskolipsku-rozhodne-se-mezi-hejtmanem-a-starostkou-lipy.html</guid><pubDate>Fri, 16 Oct 2026 14:00:00 +0200</pubDate><dc:creator>Luboš Vrabec</dc:creator><category>Politika</category><description>Také v části Libereckého kraje se rozhodne o novém senátorovi. Volí se v okrsku 36, kam spadá Českolipsko, ale také část Liberecka a Mělnicka. Do druhého kola postoupila končící starostka České Lípy Jitka Volfová (ANO) a hejtman Libereckého kraje Martin Půta (Starostové pro LK).</description></item><item><title>VIDEO: Šokující výlet s dědečkem, v České Lípě opíjel a učil kouřit děti (5 a 12)</title><link>https://liberecka.drbna.cz/spolecnost/903204-video-sokujici-vylet-s-dedeckem-v-ceske-lipe-opijel-a-ucil-kourit-deti-5-a-12.html</link><guid isPermaLink="true">https://liberecka.drbna.cz/spolecnost/903204-video-sokujici-vylet-s-dedeckem-v-ceske-lipe-opijel-a-ucil-kourit-deti-5-a-12.html</guid><pubDate>Fri, 16 Oct 2026 13:00:00 +0200</pubDate><dc:creator>Martina Petrášková</dc:creator><category>Společnost</category><description>Místo zmrzliny či dortu alkohol a tabák. Svéráznou představu rodinného výletu překazil v České Lípě v Hrnčířské ulici asistent prevence kriminality. Dědeček dával pít pivo a kouřit cigarety svým vnukům ve věku 5 a 12 let přímo na ulici. Případem se už zabývá správní orgán.</description></item><item><title>Křižovatka Sněhulák se opět uzavře. Letos už naposledy</title><link>https://liberecka.drbna.cz/doprava/903176-krizovatka-snehulak-se-opet-uzavre-letos-uz-naposledy.html</link><guid isPermaLink="true">https://liberecka.drbna.cz/doprava/903176-krizovatka-snehulak-se-opet-uzavre-letos-uz-naposledy.html</guid><pubDate>Fri, 16 Oct 2026 12:12:00 +0200</pubDate><dc:creator>Luboš Vrabec</dc:creator><category>Doprava</category><description>Křižovatku zvanou Sněhulák čeká během páteční noci poslední letošní uzavírka. Důvodem je oprava mostu silnice I/35 nad křižovatkou. Ta se uzavře v pátek v 18 hodin a uzavírka potrvá do sobotní osmé hodiny ráno.</description></item><item><title>Další krok k záchraně barokního dvora zámku Zákupy: Začíná obnova západní části</title><link>https://liberecka.drbna.cz/kultura/903165-dalsi-krok-k-zachrane-barokniho-dvora-zamku-zakupy-zacina-obnova-zapadni-casti.html</link><guid isPermaLink="true">https://liberecka.drbna.cz/kultura/903165-dalsi-krok-k-zachrane-barokniho-dvora-zamku-zakupy-zacina-obnova-zapadni-casti.html</guid><pubDate>Fri, 16 Oct 2026 11:00:00 +0200</pubDate><dc:creator>Martina Petrášková</dc:creator><category>Kultura</category><description>Na státním zámku Zákupy začala obnova západní části barokního hospodářského dvora za 242 milionů korun. Práce potrvají do roku 2029 a zajistí stavební záchranu objektu i prostory pro nový archeologický depozitář. Pokračující obnova je dalším krokem k záchraně tohoto unikátního komplexu.</description></item><item><title>Meteorologové prozradili, jaký bude podzim</title><link>https://liberecka.drbna.cz/spolecnost/903155-meteorologove-prozradili-jaky-bude-podzim.html</link><guid isPermaLink="true">https://liberecka.drbna.cz/spolecnost/903155-meteorologove-prozradili-jaky-bude-podzim.html</guid><pubDate>Fri, 16 Oct 2026 08:55:00 +0200</pubDate><dc:creator>Markéta Hamerníková</dc:creator><category>Společnost</category><description>Deštivého podzimu se zatím obávat nemusíme. Přestože o víkendu na severu Čech zaprší, výhled na dalších sedm až deset dní slibuje převážně suché počasí. Meteorologové očekávají méně srážek, než je pro toto období obvyklé.</description></item></channel></rss>

 <description><p>
	<strong>V sobotu 10. října se sklářská huť Preciosa v Kamenickém Šenově opět otevře festivalovému publiku. Benefiční projekt V žáru žen nabídne hudbu Beaty Hlavenkové, HRTL a Oskara Töröka, laserovou performance Davida Vrbíka i práci se sklem. Výtěžek večera a tichá aukce podpoří Nadační fond Ozvěna, který pomáhá dětem s trvalou ztrátou sluchu.</strong></p>

výběžek.eu https://www.vybezek.eu dobrý den ze šluknovského výběžku, konce světa - šluknovský výběžek Fri, 16 Oct 2026 10:23:12 +0000 cs hourly 1 https://wordpress.org/?v=7.1.3 https://www.vybezek.eu/wp-uploads/2018/09/cropped-favicon-vybezek-32x32.png výběžek.eu https://www.vybezek.eu 32 32 Podzimní hry 2026 – malá kopaná https://www.vybezek.eu/295858-podzimni-hry-2026-mala-kopana/ Fri, 16 Oct 2026 10:23:12 +0000 https://www.vybezek.eu/?p=295858 Ve středu 14. října 2026 se na umělém trávníku v areálu Kotliny ve Varnsdorfu uskutečnil druhý díl letošních podzimních her, tentokrát v malé kopané.

Turnaje se zúčastnila čtyři chlapecká družstva, která mezi sebou poměřila své síly systémem každý s každým. Jednotlivá utkání se hrála na 15 minut.

Naši chlapci vstupovali do turnaje s jasným cílem, kterým bylo obhájit prvenství z loňského roku. Hned v úvodním utkání proti ZŠ Východní předvedli výborný výkon a zaslouženě zvítězili vysoko 8:0. Ve druhém zápase je čekalo družstvo Gymnázia Varnsdorf. Díky skvělému vstupu do utkání a zodpovědnému výkonu si naši hráči připsali další přesvědčivé vítězství, tentokrát 4:0. V posledním utkání se naši chlapci utkali s družstvem ZŠ Edisonova. Přestože si během zápasu vytvořili řadu slibných brankových příležitostí, jejich neproměňování přineslo dramatickou koncovku. Nakonec však dokázali těsné vedení udržet a po vítězství 3:2 mohli slavit zasloužený triumf.

Naši fotbalisté tak prošli celým turnajem bez ztráty jediného bodu, s celkovým skóre 15:2, a úspěšně obhájili loňské prvenství!

Celý turnaj proběhl v přátelské a sportovní atmosféře. Všechna zúčastněná družstva si zaslouží pochvalu za předvedené výkony a nasazení. Našim chlapcům děkujeme za vzornou reprezentaci školy. Podzimní hry však pokračují dál. Již 3. 11. 2026 se uskuteční další díl, ve kterém žáci poměří své síly v plavání. Už teď se těšíme!

Mgr. Patrik Klouda, ZŠ Varnsdorf, nám. E. Beneše
